title: Codex code review: setup, pricing and how it compares
summary: Codex code review comes with ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise. How to set it up on GitHub, what /review does, and how it scores on a benchmark.
body_markdown:
Codex code review is OpenAI's AI reviewer for GitHub pull requests, plus a` /review` command in the Codex CLI, IDE extension and app, and a GitHub Action for your own workflows. PR reviews come with ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu plans, not with Free, Go or an API key, and on GitHub they post only the most serious findings, marked P0 and P1.


**Our verdict:** if your team already pays for ChatGPT, turn it on. It costs nothing extra up to your plan's limit, it's quiet by design, and AGENTS.md makes it easy to steer. But if you're serious about code review and building production applications, it isn't enough on its own. OpenAI itself calls it an additional reviewer, not a replacement for tests, branch protection or required approvals. It reports only P0 and P1 findings, has no documented way to approve or block a pull request, and draws on an allowance whose size OpenAI doesn't publish. On Martian's Code Review Bench (last-month view, checked October 10, 2026), it ranks #13 of 15 by F1.


This blog belongs to cubic (cubic.dev), an AI code review tool that competes with Codex code review, so weigh our opinions accordingly. The Codex facts here come from OpenAI's docs, help center, changelog, blog posts and GitHub repositories, and from the Codex bot's comments on OpenAI's own repository, read on October 10, 2026.

Use` /review` on your own branch before you push, and the GitHub reviewer as a second check on every pull request. Reach for the Action only if you want your own prompt, your own model choice, or API billing instead of a ChatGPT plan.


## How Codex reviews pull requests on GitHub


Codex PR reviews on GitHub come from the ChatGPT Codex Connector app, which OpenAI's[code review docs](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/code-review) call generally available. Codex reads the pull request's diff, follows the review rules in your AGENTS.md files and posts a regular GitHub review. By design, it reports only P0 and P1 findings on GitHub.


### How to turn on Codex code review


OpenAI's[GitHub setup guide](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/third-party/github) has the details. You need a ChatGPT plan that includes Codex cloud and push or admin permission on the repository.


1.


Sign in to Codex with your ChatGPT account and connect the GitHub repository. Codex cloud doesn't work with API-key sign-in.


2.


Open Codex's code review settings at app.chatgpt.com/settings/code-review and choose the repository.


3.


Turn on **Automatic review** under **Review code** . Each person can also turn on **Automatic review** under **Personal preferences** and pick a **Review trigger** .


4.


Open a pull request, or comment` @codex review` on an existing one. Codex reacts with 👀 while it works, then posts its review.


OpenAI's docs don't list when automatic reviews run. On OpenAI's own repository, the bot's help text says it reviews when a pull request is opened for review, when a draft is marked ready, and when someone comments` @codex review` . Reviews on every push aren't documented for GitHub.


### What a Codex review looks like


On OpenAI's own repository, a review opens with a short "Codex Review" note, then adds inline comments with a P0 or P1 badge, a bold title and an explanation. When a rule from AGENTS.md applies, the comment links to it.


*A P1 finding on OpenAI's own repository (*[openai/codex#51186](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/51186) *), with the "Useful?" prompt that closes its comments.*


No OpenAI page says Codex approves, requests changes or blocks a merge, and the reviews we sampled on OpenAI's repository were plain comments. The GitHub app also has read-only access to checks and statuses, so it can't post a check or commit status that branch protection could require. OpenAI recommends it as an additional reviewer, not a replacement for tests, branch protection or required approvals.

### Review rules in AGENTS.md


Codex follows the review rules in the AGENTS.md files that cover the changed code: the root file plus any nested file closer to the change. Put them under a` ## Code Review Rules` heading, grouped with` ###` headings. Rules for the whole repository go in the root file, and rules for one service go in a nested file such as` services/payments/AGENTS.md` .


```text
##  Code   Review   Rules


###  Payments
-  Amounts   are   stored    as   integer  cents  .  Flag    floats   used   for    money    in    billing  /.
-  Flag   any   payment   API   call   made   without   an   idempotency   key


```


```text
##  Code   Review   Rules


###  Payments
-  Flag   any   payment   API   call   made   without   an   idempotency   key


```


```text
##  Code   Review   Rules


###  Payments

```


OpenAI suggests starting with two or three short rules about behavior that matters in your repository, leaving formatting and lint to CI, and pruning any rule that creates noise on a test pull request. Until July 2026, its docs called this section` ## Review guidelines` ; today's docs use` ## Code Review Rules` .


OpenAI says rules make a large difference: in its primary evaluation suite, rule-guided reviews found 98% of the required custom findings, against 58.3% for the baseline control.


## The /review command in the Codex CLI


` /review` runs a dedicated reviewer on your local changes. It reads the diff, reports prioritized findings and doesn't touch your working tree. In the CLI it offers four presets: **Review against a base branch** , **Review uncommitted changes** , **Review a commit** and **Custom review instructions** . The IDE extension and the desktop app offer the first two.


For scripts and pre-push hooks,` codex review` runs the same review without the interactive menu:


```text
codex   review   -- base   main          #    review   your   branch   against   main
codex   review   -- uncommitted        #    staged  ,    unstaged   and   untracked   changes
codex   review   -- commit   1  a2b3c4     #    one   commit
codex   review   "Focus on auth and input validation"
```


```text
codex   review   -- commit   1  a2b3c4     #    one   commit
codex   review   "Focus on auth and input validation"
```


```text
codex   review   -- commit   1  a2b3c4     #    one   commit
codex   review   "Focus on auth and input validation"
```


The local reviewer's prompt is open source in the openai/codex repository; the GitHub reviewer's isn't published. The local prompt tags each finding P0 to P3, flags only bugs the change introduced, skips trivial style, and ends with a verdict that the patch is correct or incorrect, with a confidence score.` /review` uses your session's model unless you set` review_model` in` config.toml` .


Local reviews count against your plan's general Codex usage, not the separate Code Review usage that GitHub reviews draw on. With an API key, you pay API token prices.


## Codex code review in GitHub Actions


The[Codex GitHub Action](https://github.com/openai/codex-action) (` openai/codex-action@v1` , version 1.13 as of October 5, 2026) installs the Codex CLI and runs` codex exec` with a prompt you write. OpenAI's[sample workflow](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/github-action) runs when a pull request is opened, updated or reopened, and a second job posts Codex's final message as a PR comment.


The Action needs an OpenAI or Azure OpenAI API key stored as a GitHub secret, so you pay API prices rather than using your ChatGPT plan. As of October 2026, GPT-6.1 Sol costs $2.00 per million input tokens and $10.00 per million output tokens on OpenAI's API, at the Standard tier for prompts up to 272,000 input tokens.


OpenAI's security notes are worth following: by default only users with write access can trigger the Action, and you should treat PR titles and descriptions as untrusted input that could carry a prompt injection.


## Codex security review


Security Review is a deeper pass that looks only for security risks, using the diff, the repository's context and a threat model. It's a research preview on Pro, Business, Edu and Enterprise plans, not Plus. You start it with` @codex security review` , or turn on **Auto security review** for a repository and choose whether it runs when a PR opens, on every push, or whenever code review runs.


By default, automatic security reviews post High and Critical findings, and manual ones add Medium. Findings inherit the pull request's visibility, so on a public repository anyone can read them.


Codex Security, formerly Aardvark, is a separate product that scans repositories and can also review a branch's or pull request's changes for security regressions.

GitHub reviews, started automatically or with` @codex review` , draw from a separate allowance OpenAI calls Code Review usage. OpenAI doesn't publish its size today. In April 2026, its pricing page listed 20 to 50 code reviews per 5 hours on Plus; that table is gone.


Past the allowance, Plus and Pro users can buy credits, and Business, Enterprise and Edu workspaces on flexible pricing can buy workspace credits. Credits are charged by tokens, and OpenAI no longer lists a price per review.


When a repository runs out, the Codex bot says so on the pull request. On OpenAI's own repository in October 2026, it commented that "Codex usage limits have been reached for code reviews" and that "Credits must be used to enable repository wide code reviews." If you turn on automatic reviews for every pull request in a busy repository, budget for credits.


A rough example, with our arithmetic: a 10-person team on ChatGPT Business pays $2,400 a year billed yearly, and Codex code review comes with those seats, up to a limit OpenAI doesn't publish. Our[AI code review pricing comparison](https://www.cubic.dev/blog/ai-code-review-pricing) lists what other tools charge.


## Is Codex code review any good?


It catches less than the leading reviewers. On Martian's[Code Review Bench](https://codereview.withmartian.com/) (last-month view, checked October 10, 2026), the ChatGPT Codex Connector, the app that posts Codex's GitHub reviews, ranks #13 of 15 by F1, at 55.6%.


Martian, which describes itself as a research lab that doesn't sell coding tools, scores review bots on real open-source pull requests. It ranks them by F1, which combines how often developers act on a reviewer's comments with how many of the real bugs it catches. The top five, and Codex:

OpenAI says this is partly by design. In a December 2025 post, its alignment team wrote that the reviewer deliberately flags fewer issues so that more of its comments are right. Across OpenAI's own pull requests, authors changed code in response to 52.7% of the reviewer's comments. It's also one of the most used reviewers on the board: Martian's last-month view counts 498,173 of its pull requests, second only to GitHub Copilot.


Two cautions. The board moves daily: in a July 30, 2026 post, Greptile listed the Codex Connector second on the tracker at 59.4% F1. Several vendors, cubic included, have each claimed #1 at different times, and Martian warns that its data can't settle head-to-head comparisons, because bots see each other's comments and different kinds of repos adopt different tools.


## Where Codex code review falls short


-


**Only the top two priorities.** On GitHub it reports only P0 and P1 findings, so smaller problems never reach the pull request.


-


**No documented way to gate a merge.** No OpenAI page says it approves or requests changes, and the app can't post a check or commit status that branch protection could require.


-


**The allowance size isn't published.** OpenAI doesn't say how many GitHub reviews a plan includes, so you can't size a rollout before you try it.


-


**Narrow host support.** GitHub is the generally available host. OpenAI's docs have listed GitLab merge request reviews as a beta since August 2026, but one of its help articles says GitLab cloud reviews aren't available. Bitbucket and Azure DevOps aren't documented.


-


**No choice of model.** OpenAI doesn't say which model runs GitHub reviews today, and Codex cloud's default model can't be changed.


-


**No hosted option on API billing.** Teams that buy OpenAI through the API, not ChatGPT, can't use the GitHub reviewer.

In practice, the choice comes down to three things:


-


**What you already pay for.** Codex comes with ChatGPT seats your team may already have. cubic is a separate subscription.


-


**How much a review should catch.** On Martian's Code Review Bench (last-month view, checked October 10, 2026), cubic ranks #1 by F1 at 64.0% and the Codex Connector #13 at 55.6%. Martian cautions that its data can't settle head-to-head comparisons, so test both on your own pull requests.


-


**Whether the reviewer can approve.** cubic can auto-approve pull requests that meet a policy you set, after a shadow-mode trial. OpenAI documents no approvals for Codex.


## Using Codex and cubic together


They don't exclude each other. One way to split the work is Codex's` /review` on your branch before you push, and cubic on the pull request. The cubic CLI can also run local reviews on Codex models through a ChatGPT Plus or Pro plan: run` cubic auth connect codex` , sign in through the browser, then pick a Codex model in the CLI.


## Codex auto-review, skills and Claude Code


A few search terms point at features that sound like code review:


-


**Auto-review isn't code review.** Codex's Auto-review is a sandbox feature: a separate reviewer agent decides on approval requests, such as escalated commands or blocked network requests, instead of you. With ChatGPT sign-in,` codex-auto-review` is the default model behind it. It doesn't review pull requests.


-


**No general-purpose review skill.** OpenAI's skills repository has no code review skill, and` /review` is built in. Its Codex Security plugin does include` security-diff-scan` , which reviews uncommitted changes, a commit, or a branch or pull request for security regressions, and OpenAI's plugin catalog also carries CodeRabbit's plugin, which has a review skill.


-


**You can run Codex reviews from Claude Code.** OpenAI's[codex-plugin-cc](https://github.com/openai/codex-plugin-cc) adds` /codex:review` and` /codex:adversarial-review` , a read-only review that challenges design choices, tradeoffs and assumptions. It needs a ChatGPT subscription or an OpenAI API key, and its reviews count toward your Codex limits.


## Who should use Codex code review


Turn Codex code review on if:


-


Your team already has ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business or Enterprise seats and works on GitHub. It's included up to your plan's Code Review usage limit, so it adds a check to your pull requests without a separate bill until you reach that limit.


-


You want a quiet reviewer that only speaks up about serious bugs.


-


You already keep instructions in AGENTS.md and want reviews to follow them.


If you're serious about code review and building production applications, don't stop there. Codex keeps everything below P1 off the pull request, has no documented way to gate a merge, and draws on an allowance whose size OpenAI doesn't publish, so pair it with a dedicated reviewer. If you're comparing first-party reviewers, our[Claude Code review](https://www.cubic.dev/blog/claude-code-review) and[GitHub Copilot code review](https://www.cubic.dev/blog/github-copilot-code-review) guides cover the other two.


Run any reviewer on a week of your own pull requests before you trust a ranking, ours included.


If you're on GitHub, try cubic's[AI code reviewer](https://www.cubic.dev/ai-code-review) next to Codex on the same PRs. The trial lasts 7 days and needs no card.
